newsitem.title: UK: Funds seek value plays as equity markets wobble.
newsitem.headline: Funds seek value plays as equity markets wobble.

text.p: The latest wobble in stock markets around the world should prompt a further shift to value style investing, London fund managers said on Monday.
While few expect a major equity market blow-out, they said concern that the liquidity-driven rally of recent months was fading would bring more selective strategies into vogue.
"This is the classic time one would normally see value plays perform better," said Juan Nevado, strategist at Prudential Portfolio Managers.

"At the same time this is not the end of the world. We are not going to see a 1987. (But) it would be nice to have a little bit of a risk premium on assets that are risky and therefore value should out."
Analysts told Reuters the return to favour of underperforming small and mid-cap stocks, seen in many major centres, should continue relative to large capitalisation issues in coming months.
Wall Street suffered its second biggest points loss on Friday as a weak dollar and worries about U.S. profits wiped more than three percent off the Dow Jones Industrial Average.
European and Asian stocks came under pressure on Monday following the Dow slide, but were off lows in late European morning trade.
And markets face a further test of nerves this week with concerns about possible moves on interest rates at the Fed and the Bundesbank, although analysts expect no change.
Lombard Odier head of equities Tony Robinson said interest rate hikes were unlikely this week, and therefore the fundamental outlook remained positive.

The firm has done some precautionary selling in the last two weeks of Latin America and of some U.S. blue chips such as Coca Cola and Procter & Gamble. But he planned to reinvest in those markets and shares once prices dipped a bit further, as long as interest rate policy remained on hold in the U.S. and Germany.
"We see this as another periodic bout of profit-taking nervousness...There is some froth there to be taken out but nothing fundamental has changed."
Lombard was continuing to pick undervalued growth stocks, but with more emphasis on mid-cap growth rather than blue chip growth, he said.

Nevado said Prudential had been reducing equities and raising cash and cash proxies like index-linked bonds in recent months, and has been cutting back on Europe over the last few months where it feels the markets are most vulnerable.
"We are playing the value story rather than the growth story and it is really dictated by this absence of risk premiums in the European and U.S. market," he said.
Nevado said the obvious value plays at the moment were Britain and Japan, with Mexico and Australia looking relatively cheap.
He said the perception that Europe was expensive was increasingly taking hold in London's financial community.
He prefers index-linked to conventional bonds, with index linked instruments looking relatively good value in the U.S. and UK.
He said many bond markets, after adjusting for inflation, showed zero risk premium, a factor which "does make you question the short term bullishness that is in these markets".
Mike Grimble, investment strategist at Norwich Union, said equities have been due to wobble, and sees a downside of about 10 percent over the next six months.
"The markets are a touch overvalued, certainly looking at the runs in the U.S. and Europe so far this year and to some extent the UK."

But he does not see any major triggers for a marked downturn now. "A certain amount of rationality ought to return to the markets. We see it drifting lower over the next few months with no major dramatic sell off."
He said the only trigger to a major short term sell-off would be a sharp rise in U.S. short term interest rates.
